source.title: Known Results and Open Problems on C1 linearization in Banach Spaces

accepted.question_text: Let X be an infinite-dimensional C^{1,1} Banach space, and let T(x)=Ax+Χ(x) be a germ at 0 of a C^{1,1} strict contraction with A, A^{-1} ∈ L(X), Χ(0)=0, and DΧ(0)=0. Is every such contraction germ locally C^1-linearizable near 0, meaning that there exists a C^1 local change of coordinates R(x)=x+φ(x) with φ(0)=0 and Dφ(0)=0 such that RTR^{-1}=A, even without the non-resonance or spectral-gap assumptions used in the known infinite-dimensional linearization theorems?

evidence.quote: Theorem 3. (C1 linearization of contractions, H.M.R. and J. S.-M., 2004, [12]) Let X be a C1,1 Banach space and A, A−1 ∈ L(X). Let ν−i, ν+i, i = 1, . . . , n be such that: ... Let X = X(x) be a C1,1-function in a neighborhood of the origin, such that X(0) = 0, DX(0) = 0. Then, for the map Tx = Ax + X(x) there exists a C1-map Rx = x + φ(x) satisfying φ(0) = 0, Dφ(0) = 0, such that RTR−1 = A in a sufficiently small neighborhood of the origin.

Despite of the fact that we were sorry for not having been aware of these independent works, in some sense, the coincidence of the three lines of research in that a non-resonance condition like the condition ν+1/ν+i < ν−i, i = 1, . . . , n of (2), or the condition 1 in Theorem 2 should be really necessary. Our interest in this point was reinforced by the following sentence written in [1] as the last phrase in the paper: Apparently, it is not known whether every C1,1 strict contraction germ in an infinite dimensional space is C1-linearizable.

accepted.question_text: For the problem of C^1 linearization of contractions on infinite-dimensional Banach spaces, can one construct sharper counterexamples than the existing ones? In particular, is there a counterexample of the type described after Theorem 6 with r=0, or even a counterexample whose linear part A has spectral modulus set |σ(A)| = [ab,b] ∪ {a} for some real numbers 0 < b < a < 1?

evidence.quote: Problem 1: Better counter-examples. A better understanding of the non-resonance conditions (2) needs better counterexamples. It would be good to have a counterexample as in Theorem 6 but with r = 0. Or, even better, a counterexample with |σ(A)| = [ab, b]∪ {a}, with 0 < b < a < 1.

accepted.question_text: The known counterexamples to C^1 linearization described in this paper use an infinite-dimensional Jordan block in the linear part. Is such a Jordan-block structure actually necessary for counterexamples? More specifically, can one build counterexamples in which the linear part A is selfadjoint; and if that is impossible, can the spectral non-resonance condition (2) be improved when A is selfadjoint, or more generally when A is normal?
accepted.context_brief: Role of Jordan blocks and selfadjointness

evidence.quote: Problem 2: Jordan blocks. Our counterexamples have an infinite-dimensional Jordan block. Is this necessary? Can one have counterexamples with a selfadjoint linear part A? If this is not the case, can one improve (2) if A is selfadjoint, or even normal?

accepted.question_text: Suppose the nonlinear part in a local map T(x)=Ax+X(x) on an infinite-dimensional Banach space vanishes to order higher than two near the fixed point, for example X(x)=O(|x|^{1+η}) with η>0 instead of merely X(x)=O(|x|^2). Do such higher-order nonlinearities permit weaker spectral restrictions on the linear part A than the non-resonance condition (2) required in the C^1 linearization theorem stated as Theorem 3?

evidence.quote: Problem 3: Higher order nonlinearities. As it is seen in the statement of Theorem 3 it is considered that the nonlinearity X(x) vanishes together with its first derivative at x = 0. Since the nonlinearity is of class C1,1 this amounts to say that X(x) = O(|x|2). As it happens in Theorem 2 one can expect that larger values of η if X(x) = O(|x|1+η) would give less restrictive conditions on σ(A) in (2). This deserves to be studied.

Observe that η is restricted to be positive, but otherwise can be large. It is easy to see that the inequality ||A−1|| ||A||1+η < 1 is satisfied by an equivalent norm ... if and only if |σ(A)| is contained in an open interval of the form (a−, a+) with (a+)1+η < a−. So, the restrictions on σ(A) become weaker when the order of the nonlinearity near zero becomes larger. This will give rise to one of the open problems below.

accepted.question_text: If one tries to weaken the spectral restrictions for C^1 linearization in the presence of higher-order nonlinearities, what are the actual limits of such improvements? In particular, can one construct counterexamples for maps whose nonlinear part has order 1+η with η>0, showing where any less restrictive spectral conditions must fail?

evidence.quote: Problem 4: Counter-examples for higher order nonlinearities. At the same time as one could work on solving Problem 3 one should look for counterexamples, to see if there are limits to these less restrictive conditions.
In the directions of this last Problem 4 we present here a small new result. It is just a generalization of Theorem 6 above to different order nonlinearities.
